title: Manna (Exodus 16)
hookLine: bread from heaven, enough for each day, and a double portion before Shabbat

lines: BACK IN EGYPT WE ATE OUR FILL.
BREAD FROM THE SKY, ONE DAY AT A TIME.
cards: Open a fridge and look at it the way a desert traveler would. Leftovers in the back you forgot about. Three kinds of mustard.
A lot of us stock up, just in case, because tomorrow feels uncertain. A month out of Egypt, the Israelites are in the wilderness, and the food from Egypt has run out.
They complain: back in Egypt we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill. And God answers with a strange promise: bread will fall from the sky every morning. But you can only take enough for today.

teach.b: God says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Behold, I will cause to rain bread from heaven for you." Next morning the dew lifts, and on the ground there's something fine and flaky, like frost.
The people say to each other, man hu? What is it? "For they knew not what it was."
The name sticks: man, manna, is basically the word what. They ate a question for forty years. The Torah says it was white, like coriander seed, and tasted like wafers made with honey.
The rabbis added that it tasted like whatever each person wanted. Now the rules. Each person gathers about an omer, a measure of a day's food.
Some gather more, some less, and when they measure it, nobody has too much and nobody too little. Don't keep any until morning. Some people do anyway, and by morning it's full of worms and stinks.
On the sixth day, everyone finds twice as much, and the extra keeps overnight, because on the seventh day nothing falls.

teach.h: NONE LEFT OVER, EXCEPT FOR SHABBAT.
teach.b: So in the wilderness the people keep a Shabbat, and it comes with a double portion. Tradition links that to the two loaves on the Shabbat table today; more on them later.
The rabbis saw manna as a daily school of trust. You couldn't hoard it. You had to go out each morning and find there was enough, again.

teach.h: I WILL CAUSE TO RAIN BREAD FROM HEAVEN.
teach.b: Moses later puts it this way: people don't live by bread alone. And a jar of manna, the story says, was kept for future generations to see.

how: Jews recall the manna every Shabbat with two loaves of challah on the table, and some say a reading about the manna in daily prayers as a lesson in trust.

o: sweet sap the Israelites tapped from desert trees
bread from heaven, named for asking what is it?
quail the wind blew into the camp at evening

games.q: what's inside the manna — tap the pairs.

s: the word manna comes from a question
the people saw it and said man hu, what is it?
whoever gathered more had extra left over
when they measured, nobody had too much and nobody had too little.
manna fell on the seventh day too
none fell on Shabbat; a double portion came on the sixth day and kept overnight.

games.q: you've gathered your manna, and there's a little left over tonight. you're worried about tomorrow. what do you do?
o: keep it for the morning, just in case.
eat what you need and leave none.
games.why: the rule was leave none until morning. those who kept it found worms. only the sixth day's double portion kept, for Shabbat.

practice: Think of one thing you tend to over-gather: food, clothes, tabs open on your phone, worry about next week. Hold it up to the manna rule, enough for today and no more, and ask what enough looks like, just for today.
Then set the rest down for now, like a bag you've been carrying for no reason.

wordCard.voice: Manna. From man hu, what is it? Bread from heaven, gathered each morning, enough for one day, and double before Shabbat.

orig.note: Hebrew: manna. the people's question, man hu, what is it, became its name.

carryVoice: Your line: enough for today. Each morning in the wilderness, there was enough again. Ninety-two days in.
